Getting started with featR

Source: vignettes/featR.Rmd
featR.Rmd

What featR is for

Feature selection in R is spread across a dozen packages, each with its own calling convention and its own idea of what a result looks like. Comparing two methods means learning two APIs and writing glue code to line up the answers.

featR wraps 14 selection methods behind one calling convention and one return type, so swapping fs_lasso() for fs_boruta() is a one-word change. The methods cover statistical filters, regularized and tree-based models, and wrappers that refit a model per candidate subset. Two dimensionality-reduction helpers, fs_pca() and fs_svd(), share the calling convention but not the return type.

Installing

The released version is on CRAN:

install.packages("featR")

The development version is on GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("elkronos/featR")

featR itself depends only on data.table, withr, and base R. The modeling engines (glmnet, caret, Boruta, randomForest, brms, and others) are in Suggests. A function that needs one checks when you call it and stops with the install.packages() line you need. Optional dependencies has one command that installs all of them.

The calling convention

Every selection function takes the data first and the name of the outcome column second:

fs_<method>(data, target, <method options>, ...)

Housekeeping arguments come last. Every function takes verbose. Functions that use randomness take seed = NULL, and functions that can run in parallel take n_cores, parallel, or both. The four methods with no outcome, fs_correlation(), fs_unsupervised(), fs_pca(), and fs_svd(), drop target. fs_svd() calls its input x, because it takes a matrix rather than a table of observations.

featR runs sequentially unless you ask for parallel workers, and caps any request at the cores the machine has. It never touches your random number generator unless you pass seed, and then restores the previous state when the call returns. Reproducibility and parallelism has the details.

Every selection function returns an fs_result, and selected() pulls the kept feature names out of any of them. fs_pca() and fs_svd() reduce dimensions rather than choose variables, so they return their own decomposition lists instead.

A worked example

This example predicts mpg in mtcars from the other ten columns. It uses two filters, both of which run with no suggested packages installed.

fs_supervised() scores each feature against the target on its own: absolute Pearson correlation when the target is numeric, a one-way ANOVA F statistic when it is categorical. The two scales differ (|r| runs from 0 to 1, F has no upper bound), so a threshold that suits one is meaningless for the other. Keep the features with |r| above 0.5:

relevant <- fs_supervised(mtcars, target = "mpg", threshold = 0.5)
relevant
#> <fs_result> supervised_correlation (regression)
#> Selected 8 of 10 features
#>   cyl, disp, hp, drat, wt, vs, am, carb
#> Details: mask, indices, filtered, threshold, direction, action, n_features (in $details)

Eight of the ten columns pass. gear (|r| = 0.48) and qsec (0.42) fall below the cut. The scores sit in relevant$scores:

round(sort(relevant$scores, decreasing = TRUE), 2)
#>   wt  cyl disp   hp drat   vs   am carb gear qsec 
#> 0.87 0.85 0.85 0.78 0.68 0.66 0.60 0.55 0.48 0.42

A filter that looks at one feature at a time cannot see that two survivors carry the same information. cyl and disp both score 0.85 here, and they are correlated 0.90 with each other. fs_correlation() ignores the outcome and looks only at how the features relate to one another. With prune = TRUE, the default, it drops features one at a time until no remaining pair is correlated above the threshold:

pruned <- fs_correlation(mtcars[, selected(relevant)], threshold = 0.8)
pruned$details$dropped
#> [1] "cyl"  "disp"

It dropped cyl and disp. summary() shows the call and a ranked score table, with an asterisk on each feature that was kept. For fs_correlation(), a feature’s score is its largest absolute correlation with any other input feature, dropped ones included. So wt (0.89 with disp) and hp (0.83 with cyl) score above 0.8 and survive anyway, because their partners were dropped.

summary(pruned)
#> <fs_result> correlation_pearson
#> Selected 6 of 8 features
#>   hp, drat, wt, vs, am, carb
#> Details: corr_matrix, pairs, dropped, redundant, n_features (in $details)
#> 
#> Call:
#>   fs_correlation(data = mtcars[, selected(relevant)], threshold = 0.8)
#> 
#> Scores (8 features, ranked):
#>  feature  score selected
#>     drat 0.7127        *
#>       am 0.7127        *
#>     carb 0.7498        *
#>       vs 0.8108        *
#>       hp 0.8324        *
#>       wt 0.8880        *
#>      cyl 0.9020         
#>     disp 0.9020         
#> (* = selected)

selected() returns the final set, ready to pass to a model:

keep <- selected(pruned)
keep
#> [1] "hp"   "drat" "wt"   "vs"   "am"   "carb"
fit <- lm(reformulate(keep, response = "mpg"), data = mtcars)

fs_supervised() looked at mpg to choose these six columns, so any error estimate for fit computed on the same 32 rows is optimistic. Run the selection on training rows only and score the model on rows it never saw. Validation and leakage shows how, and lists which numbers featR reports are honest held-out estimates.

To try another method, change the function and its options. With glmnet installed, the lasso version of the same question is:

lasso <- fs_lasso(mtcars, target = "mpg", seed = 1)
selected(lasso)
#> [1] "wt"   "cyl"  "hp"   "am"   "carb" "drat"

The fs_result object covers the seven components, how to read print() and summary(), what scores means for each method, how to compare results side by side, and what to do when nothing is selected.

The four families

Family Functions Guide
Filters fs_unsupervised(), fs_supervised(), fs_correlation(), fs_chi(), fs_infogain() Filter methods
Regularization and embedded importance fs_lasso(), fs_elastic(), fs_randomforest(), fs_mars() Regularization and embedded importance
Wrappers fs_recursivefeature(), fs_svm(), fs_boruta(), fs_stepwise(), fs_bayes() Wrapper methods
Dimensionality reduction fs_pca(), fs_svd() Dimensionality reduction

Where to go next

If you are not sure which function fits your data, start with Choosing a method. It pairs common questions with functions and has a table of what each function accepts: task type, data types, missing values, and which suggested package it needs.

Before you report any number from a selection, read Validation and leakage. The full list of functions and arguments is in the reference.
